client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. There's this coffee shop she loved that we used to go to together, and every time I pass by it or even think about going in, I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I'm really glad you did. The way that coffee shop carries so much of her presence makes complete sense; places can hold grief in such a tender, unexpected way. What do you notice happening in your body or your thoughts in the moment when that wave of sadness hits you?

client: It's like my chest gets really tight and I suddenly feel kind of hollow, like there's this empty space where something used to be. My mind goes straight to specific memories, like the way she'd always order the same thing and save half of it for me, and then I feel guilty for even thinking about going in there without her, like it would be some kind of betrayal. I don't know if that makes sense, but it's like the sadness and the guilt kind of pile on top of each other at the same time.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and the way you describe it — that hollow feeling alongside the guilt — shows just how much love is wrapped up in this grief. That thought that going back would be a "betrayal" is really worth gently exploring, because it's doing a lot of heavy lifting in keeping you away from something that also holds beautiful memories of her. What do you think your grandmother would actually feel if she knew you went back to that coffee shop?

client: Rationally, I know she'd probably want me to go back, she was never the type to want people to be sad on her account. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it are two completely different things, because when I imagine walking through that door alone, it doesn't feel like honoring her, it just feels like a reminder that she's gone. I guess I'm not sure how thinking about what she'd want is supposed to make the hollow feeling go away.
therapist: You've just named something really important in CBT — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is real, and just thinking differently doesn't instantly dissolve the pain, so you're not doing anything wrong. The hollow feeling isn't a sign that the thought work isn't true; it's grief doing what grief does, and it moves at its own pace. I'm curious — when you imagine being in that coffee shop alone, is the story your mind is telling you purely one of loss, or is there any small part of the memory of *her* that might also be present there with you?

client: I think if I'm being honest, both things are true at the same time, like she would be there in the sense that everything in that place reminds me of her, but I'm not sure if that's comforting or if it would just make the loss feel more sharp and real. It's hard to imagine sitting at one of those tables and feeling her presence as something warm rather than just as an absence. I guess I'm scared that if I go in and it just feels empty, it'll somehow take away the good memories I have of being there with her.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — you're protecting something precious, and the worry that reality might overwrite a beautiful memory is a really tender place to be. It's worth noticing though that your mind is treating this as a certainty, that it *will* feel empty, when actually you can't know yet what you'd find there. What might it mean for those memories if the visit turned out to hold both the ache *and* some warmth at the same time — do you think that would make them less real, or possibly even more?

client: I hadn't really thought about it that way, like maybe both feelings could exist at the same time without one canceling out the other. But I think part of me is also worried that I'd fall apart in a public place, and that feels embarrassing and overwhelming to even consider. I don't know if I'm ready to just walk in there and find out, it feels like a big ask.
therapist: You're already doing something really meaningful just by sitting with the idea of it, and "not ready yet" is a completely valid place to be — this doesn't have to be all or nothing. The fear of falling apart publicly is so understandable, but it might also be worth noticing that grief showing up in that way wouldn't be weakness; it would just be love with nowhere to go. If walking straight in feels like too big a step right now, is there a smaller way you could imagine getting a little closer to it — maybe just pausing outside, or going at a quiet time with someone you trust?

client: The idea of just pausing outside feels a little more manageable than walking straight in, but I also don't really have someone I'd want to bring with me because most of my friends didn't know my grandmother that well and I'd feel like I had to explain everything. I think the loneliness of it is actually a big part of what makes it so hard, like grief is already isolating and the idea of doing something that emotional without anyone who really gets it just amplifies that. Maybe pausing outside on my own is something I could try, but I'm honestly not sure I won't just avoid walking past that street altogether.
therapist: The loneliness you're describing is such a real and painful layer of grief — not just missing her, but missing having someone who *knew* her and could hold that with you. It makes complete sense that facing the coffee shop alone feels heavier because of that, and avoiding the street isn't a failure, it's just where you are right now. I'm wondering though — when you imagine pausing outside on your own, is there a way you could bring a small piece of connection with you, like maybe going with the intention of thinking one specific thing you'd want to tell her, almost like a quiet moment that's just between the two of you?

client: That actually does feel a little different from just showing up and hoping for the best, like having a specific intention gives it some kind of purpose instead of just standing there feeling lost. But I'm also aware that I'm the kind of person who plans things and then finds a reason not to do them when the moment comes, so I'm not sure I trust myself to actually follow through. I guess I'm wondering if it's okay to just sit with the idea for now without committing to a timeline, because pressure makes me shut down even more.
therapist: It's absolutely okay to sit with the idea for now — in fact, honoring what you know about yourself, that pressure makes you shut down, is actually a really wise and self-aware thing to do rather than a sign of avoidance. The intention itself has value even before you act on it, and there's no deadline on grief. I'm curious, just gently — what would it feel like to simply let this idea exist without any pressure, knowing you can come back to it whenever it feels right?

client: Honestly, that feels like a bit of a relief to hear, because I think I came in here half expecting to be given some kind of assignment I'd feel bad about not completing. Letting it just exist without a deadline takes some of the weight off, though I notice there's still a small voice in the back of my head saying that "sitting with it" is just a nicer way of saying I'm going to keep avoiding it forever. I guess I'm not totally sure how I'd know the difference between giving myself space and just letting fear win.
therapist: That little voice is actually really useful — it shows a part of you genuinely wants to move through this, not just around it, and that's worth trusting. The difference between space and avoidance often comes down to whether you're still gently facing the idea or whether you've stopped letting yourself think about it altogether — and the fact that you're here, talking about it, already puts you on the facing-it side. I'm wondering, do you notice any difference in how you feel about the coffee shop now compared to when you first walked in today?

client: I think there is a small difference, like the coffee shop feels slightly less like a threat and a little more like just a place that holds something important, though I wouldn't say the sadness has lifted much. It's more that I feel less alone in thinking about it right now, which I wasn't expecting because I came in pretty skeptical that talking would actually do anything. I guess I'm just aware that this feeling might not last once I leave here and go back to my regular day.
therapist: That shift — from threat to "a place that holds something important" — is actually more significant than it might feel right now, and it's something *you* did by being willing to look at it differently. It's completely natural to worry that the feeling won't last, but what you've touched on today doesn't disappear; it's more like you've quietly added something to how you're able to hold this grief. As you head back into your day, what's one small thing you could remind yourself of if the heavier feelings come back?

client: I think I'd want to remind myself that the sadness and the warmth can exist at the same time, that one doesn't cancel out the other, because that was the thing that actually shifted something for me today. But I'm also a little worried that in the moment when the grief hits hard, I won't be able to access that thought, it'll just feel like words I heard once in a therapy session. I guess I'm not sure how you make something like that stick when your emotions are running the show.
therapist: That's such a real and honest concern — insight can feel slippery when emotions are intense, and it's not a flaw in you, it's just how the brain works under stress. One thing that can help is anchoring the thought to something sensory and concrete, so instead of trying to recall words, you might connect it to a specific image of her, like the way she'd save half her order for you, because that memory already *holds* both the love and the loss at the same time. Would it feel meaningful to choose one small memory like that as a kind of anchor you could return to — something that lives in your body a little more than just a thought?
